claims.claim_vector_01: Opposing forces have opposite signs when summed along one axis.
claims.claim_net_force_01: Net force is the vector sum of all forces on an object.
claims.claim_n2l_01: Newton's second law relates net force, mass, and acceleration as F_net = ma.
claims.claim_balanced_01: Constant velocity is consistent with zero net force.
claims.claim_mass_01: For the same net force, doubling mass halves acceleration.

items.prompt: A 3 N force acts right and a 1 N force acts left. What is the net force magnitude?
items.explanation: Treat right as positive: 3 - 1 = 2 N to the right.

items.prompt: A cart moves at constant velocity. What is its net force in newtons?
items.explanation: Constant velocity means zero acceleration, so the net force is 0 N.

hints.text: Use acceleration, not speed, in F = ma.

items.prompt: A 2 kg object has a 6 N net force. What is its acceleration magnitude?
A 4 kg box has 18 N right and 6 N left. What is its acceleration magnitude?
items.explanation: Net force is 12 N right, so acceleration is 12 / 4 = 3 m/s² right.

hints.text: Find net force before dividing by mass.

items.prompt: A 5 kg cart is pushed 25 N right against 10 N friction. What is its acceleration magnitude?
items.explanation: Net force is 15 N right. Divide by 5 kg to get 3 m/s².

hints.text: Combine forces with their directions before using F = ma.
The net force is 25 - 10. Divide that result by mass.

items.prompt: A 4 kg object has 18 N right and 6 N left. Find acceleration magnitude.
items.explanation: Subtract opposing forces, then use a = F_net / m.

items.prompt: The approved force diagram shows 20 N right and 5 N left on 5 kg. Find acceleration magnitude.
items.explanation: The diagram gives 15 N net force, so acceleration is 3 m/s².

hints.text: Use the arrow directions to find net force.

items.prompt: Goal: resolve horizontal forces, then calculate acceleration.
items.explanation: We will separate the two jobs so each step stays visible.

items.prompt: First find the vector sum of forces. Only then use F_net = ma.
items.explanation: This order prevents a single applied force from being mistaken for net force.

items.prompt: Worked example: 10 N right, 4 N left, mass 2 kg.
items.explanation: Net force = 6 N right; acceleration = 6 / 2 = 3 m/s² right.

items.prompt: Read the approved free-body diagram from arrows to equation.
items.explanation: Sum signed arrow values to get net force, then divide by mass.

items.prompt: Recap: explain why opposing force magnitudes are subtracted before applying F = ma.
items.explanation: Forces are vectors; opposite directions use opposite signs.

items.prompt: Resolve net force before using a = F_net / m.
items.explanation: The acceleration follows the direction of the net force.

items.prompt: Check: did you combine every horizontal force before dividing by mass?
items.explanation: The verified procedure is net force first, acceleration second.

items.prompt: Principle: resolve F_net, then apply F_net = ma.
items.explanation: Keep sign and direction through both operations.

items.prompt: A 2 kg cart has 8 N net force for 2 s, then 4 N net force. What is the second-stage acceleration?
items.explanation: Acceleration in the second stage is 4 / 2 = 2 m/s².

hints.text: Use only the second-stage net force.

items.prompt: Which false assumption would make someone use 8 N in the second stage?
items.explanation: It would incorrectly assume the first-stage force persists after the force changes.

items.prompt: For the same net force, what happens to acceleration when mass doubles?
items.explanation: Acceleration halves because a = F_net / m.
